verdicts.measurement: My own code is in verify-photo/measure.py, with the numbers in verify-photo/measurements.txt. (1) Plain light area: v5 is 40.9 % of the frame and 64.1 % of the upper half; v4 is 28.8 % and 43.5 %. The v5 fifths are 77/58/32/16/21. Stricter and looser thresholds give v5 38.9-44.0 % and v4 26.5-32.1 %, so the gap is robust. Masks: plainmask-v4-v5-mine.png. (2) Window frames are at x 1062-1097 and 1463-1516 in v5, and 742-790 and 1197-1254 in v4. Garden in v5: 145 px through the left window (x 865-1010, then a grey jamb and the frame) plus about 45-80 px through the right one. v4 shows about 580 px. (3) Ball: centre x 722 (0.451 W) and y 1111 (0.555 H), r 172, top at y 939, so 47 % of the height lies above it. (4) Book: the page block's front-right corner is at x 1572-1574, 26-28 px from the edge (13-14 px at 800 wide, 8 px at 480). The end face shows from x 1574 to 1600. The back-right corner, extrapolated, is near x 1740, outside the frame. Crops: v5-book-rightend-3x.png, v5-web800-rightedge-2xnn.png, v5-web480-rightedge-4xnn.png. In v4 the whole book was in frame, but its back-right corner was at about x 1595, nearly touching the edge (v4-web480-rightedge-4xnn.png). (5) The table's left edge is at x 270 from y 1340 to 1990.
verdicts.reasoning: The numbers reproduce, and the book clip is a real edge fault. At 800 and 480 the frame cuts the book just past its front-right corner, leaving a sliver of end face that looks unplanned. I confirm that part. The case for blocking does not hold. (a) The critic writes that the frame still reads as a real photograph of a home with the Core clearly the subject. That rules out every blocking test except 'fails as a living-space photograph', and it does not fail that test. At 480 it reads as a daylit corner of a room with two windows, a side table, a glass and a book. (b) 'The window that carried by day is now mostly gone' is overstated. The left window still runs the full height above the table with bright garden, and the right window shows garden above its sill. (c) No seating, rug, art or floor showed in v4 either, so the move did not cause that, and the proposed shift would not add any of it. (d) The critic's own weight map puts the centre of mass at 0.57 in v4 and 0.59 in v5. The balance barely moved; what changed is that window became plain wall. (e) How much negative space to leave is a composition preference, though more wall does pull against 'rich grounds'. So: fix the book edge, and treat the amount of wall as a note. Caution on the proposed fix: a lens shift of 250 px puts the table's left edge (x 270) at x 20, which makes a new sliver at the left edge. 200 px leaves 70 px. Getting the whole book in needs about 170 px or more, because its back-right corner is near x 1740. Check the left edge as well as the newly revealed right side.

verdicts.measurement: The coincidence the critic measured reproduces. At y 1330-1500 the glass's bright right wall ends at x 1271-1274 and the book starts at x 1274-1277. But that line is the glass's own outline hiding the book, not the book's end. I traced the book's straight edges. The cover's left edge runs from the visible back-left corner (1381, 1245) along y = -0.824x + 2383 into the glass at (1276, 1332), and the front edge runs along y = 0.218x + 1149.5. The two lines meet at the hidden front-left corner, x 1184, y 1407. That is 88 px behind (left of) the glass's right wall, so 22 % of the book's front width is behind the glass. The book's contact line is at about y 1475 at the glass's centre, while the glass's foot is at about y 1510-1570. So the glass stands about 35 px, a few centimetres, in front of the book. Crops: v5-glass-book-join-3x.png, v5-glass-foot-vs-book-2x-annot.png, v5-web800-group-2xnn.png, v5-web480-group-3xnn.png. Scale of the 6 cm move: the front-right corner went from x 1428 in v4 to 1572 (144 px), and the back-left corner from about 1265 to 1381 (116 px). That is about 21 px per cm at the hidden corner.
verdicts.reasoning: There is no tangent here, only a clear overlap. The book's diagonal left edge visibly runs behind the glass below the rim. Its refracted image shows inside the glass, which is physically right. The glass's foot sits clearly lower than the book's, so the depth order reads unambiguously at 800 and at 480. The finding's key premise, that the book's corner is hidden just behind the glass edge, is wrong by 88 px. Any overlap would show the same 0 px gap. The proposed fix would also create the very fault it describes. Moving the book 'a further 3-4 cm' takes the hidden corner to x 1247-1268, 4-25 px behind the glass wall, which is a true near-tangent. A clear 15-25 px strip would need about 5-5.5 cm. That would push the book's front-right corner (x 1572 plus about 120 px) out of frame unless the frame also moves. Leaving the book where it is, the overlap is good.

verdicts.reasoning:
The observation holds. In my 800 and 480 crops the ball reads vermilion and the base a darker brick-maroon, where the studio reads as one crimson. The step reproduces exactly (12.7 / 18.4 / 6.4). On reflection-free body patches the room's step is still nearly double the studio's (about 10 against 5.6), so the ball's window reflections do not explain it. The base is unchanged since v4. The face does darken toward the foot (35.6 to 30.1 to 26.3) where the studio's lightens (35.8 to 39.5).

Corrections that lower the weight:
(1) The second cause is misregistered. The studio has the same paler rose band at the bullnose, and it is lighter there (45.0/52.1/27.5 against the room's 41.0/44.6/32.0). The critic's 36.2/57.5 is the studio's upper face, because the proportional row map missed the band.
(2) The darkening is right physics, as the critic half-concedes. The lower skirt faces brown wood in shade (L* 47, hue 58); the studio's faces a white floor (L* 82). The warm shift at the foot (hue 34 to 41) happens inside one frame and one view transform, so it is the wood's bounce, not AgX. The coordinator's dome test already found the base model right.
(3) Inside the frame the lower face keeps the ball's hue (41.1 against 42.6). This is the same red in shade on a satin skin; at L* 26 it reads maroon-brown. It does not misstate the tint.
(4) The expected target, studio L* 36-40 and hue 31-34 at the foot, asks for studio numbers beside a brown table. A camera-side fill would also show in the polished ball unless it were hidden from glossy rays, which risks the worse fault, looking unreal.

It reads as a real photograph and does not change the color's identity. It is visible at web size, but it is the light of this scene, not a render fault. Worth knowing as a lighting choice, and a deeper Core pour would narrow it. Severity: note, not fix.
